title: Redwood structured output & function-calling demo
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Orion Analytics through JSON-mode structured output and function/tool-calling. Demo showed schema validation, guarded outputs, and how Console/Optimize suggest quantization and batching profiles. Customer cares about predictable latency, schema guarantees for downstream systems, and private deployment options for PII. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot + benchmark; Redwood to share security pack and pilot pricing.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-08-09 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Ava Patel (Redwood Product), Liam Chen (Orion Head of ML), Priya Rao (Orion CTO), Jorge Alvarez (Orion Lead Platform Eng), Nia Brooks (Orion PM)

Auto-generated Summary (may be rough): Quick demo of Redwood JSON-mode structured output and function calling. Touched on guardrails, schema enforcement, and how Console shows per-route latency/cost. Customer asked about private deployments, data retention, and how to keep downstream systems from breaking on schema drift.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Sofia, AE at Redwood, with Marcus our SE and Ava from Product. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya: Good, thanks. We are excited to see the structured output stuff — our pipelines break a lot if the model changes shape.
[00:15] Marcus: Totally. Today we'll show JSON mode with schema validation and tool/function calling that prevents malformed outputs. We'll also flip over to Console to show latency/route dashboards and then Optimize for batching/quantization suggestions.
[00:30] Liam: Awesome. Our main concerns are guaranteed schema (we have downstream DB loaders), consistent latency under load, and PII handling.
[00:38] Marcus: Noted. We'll call out where dedicated or private helps for PII and latency.
[00:43] Sofia: Quick agenda: 1) short architecture recap, 2) live demo (JSON output + function calling), 3) Console + Optimize tour, 4) Q&A and next steps.
[01:00] Jorge: Can you start with the architecture? We have a hybrid infra and some on-prem data stores.
[01:07] Marcus: Sure. At a high level Redwood has a serving runtime that handles kernel selection, KV cache, and batching. For customers who need isolation you can choose Dedicated reserved pools or Private VPC deploys. For this demo we'll use a hosted model but show how you can pin versions and route to private endpoints.
[01:25] Priya: When you say KV cache, do you mean client-side or on the serving node?
[01:30] Marcus: On the serving node — we manage KV cache to speed up autoregressive calls and reduce token costs. There's also prefix caching for common prompts.
[01:38] Nia: Ok cool. Ready for the demo.
[01:42] Marcus: I'm sharing my screen now.
[01:45] [screen share starts]
[02:10] Marcus: Here is the JSON mode example. We set a schema and instruct the model to return a JSON object that matches fields: id, intent, entities[], confidence, and actions[]. We also attach a function definition for tool-calling — for example, a call to your enrichment service or a database upsert.
[02:30] Marcus: Note the schema guardrails — if the model returns something that doesn't validate, Redwood can 1) reject and return an error, 2) attempt a repair pass, or 3) fall back to a simpler model variant.
[02:48] Liam: Repair pass meaning you send the content back to the model to reformat? That sounds expensive.
[02:54] Marcus: It can be. We surface tradeoffs: a strict reject is cheapest and safest; a repair pass can salvage output but adds latency. Optimize can recommend which route by looking at historical error rates and cost budgets.
[03:10] Priya: Show us the function calling flow.
[03:15] Marcus: Sure. I'll trigger an intent 'create_ticket' in the schema. The model returns structured JSON with parameters; Redwood then auto-maps that to a function call payload. You can set auth headers and URL templates in Console.
[03:33] [demo runs: model returns JSON]
[03:40] Marcus: You can see the model produced actions[0] = {"type":"create_ticket","payload":{...}}. Console highlights the call and shows whether the function succeeded. If it failed, there's an automatic retry policy.
[03:55] Nia: Do you allow custom validation hooks? We want to run extra checks before invoking internal services.
[04:01] Marcus: Yes — Console supports pre-call validators and you can plug in a lambda or webhook. There's an option to run validation inside Private deployments for sensitive data.
[04:14] Liam: How do you prevent the model from hallucinating fields or inventing IDs?
[04:18] Marcus: Two layers: the schema enforcement plus a deterministic sanitizer that can block patterns (like freeform html) and require specific types. Also you can mark fields as enums; the model is constrained to those values and if it deviates we treat as validation error.
[04:34] Sofia: Quick detour — pricing tradeoffs. For heavy realtime traffic you may want Dedicated to guarantee latency SLOs; hosted is more elastic. Thoughts?
[04:45] Priya: Our use case is near-realtime enrichment for analytics pipelines, 95th percentile latency < 150ms ideally.
[04:52] Marcus: For sub-150ms at scale you'll look at Dedicated with optimized kernels and smaller sequence lengths. We can model this in a bench run.
[05:05] Jorge: What about quantization? We saw earlier that quantization can blow up latency sometimes.
[05:10] Ava: We recommend quant profiles per workload. Optimize will surface candidate quantization levels and predicted throughput/latency impacts. For low-latency critical routes we sometimes use FP16 or int8 profiles tuned for the model and sequence length.
[05:26] [10 min mark — demo continues with sample prompts]
[10:05] Marcus: Here's a real sample prompt from Liam's team (thanks). We'll run it and show the Console trace — you can see token breakdown, per-stage timing, and cost.
[10:18] [model returns JSON, Console shows trace]
[10:25] Marcus: Notice the KV cache hit on the prefix which reduces token generation. Console flagged a small schema warning — it returned an extra null in entities[].
[10:36] Ava: In Console you can drill into individual requests and re-run them in a sandbox to test guardrail changes. We keep a history for debugging regressions tied to test prompts.
[10:48] Liam: That history sounds great. How long is the audit log kept? We have retention rules.
[10:54] Marcus: Hosted defaults to 90 days but Enterprise/Private can customize retention or disable retention. We can also redact PII at ingestion or use customer-managed keys.
[11:08] Priya: Tell us more about KMS/HSM integration.
[11:12] Marcus: For Private deployments we support customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK) and HSM integrations for key custody. Hosted can integrate with BYOK but with different SLAs. We'll send architecture docs.
[11:22] Nia: Back to function calling — can we map multiple function names to different downstream services and have Redwood route based on confidence?
[11:30] Marcus: Yes. You can configure routing policies: confidence thresholds, fallback functions, or route to manual review. Console's rollout control can also A/B different function handlers.
[11:44] Jorge: If a function triggers a DB write and the model misclassifies, can you do transactional rollback?
[11:50] Marcus: Redwood doesn't manage your DB transactions; we recommend the enrichment function be idempotent and include a pre-write validation. For Private you can place validation closer to source to reduce blast radius.
[12:05] Priya: How do you handle schema evolution? Our downstream teams will add fields.
[12:12] Marcus: We support versioned schemas. Console shows active schema per route and you can pin versions or roll out canary schema to a subset of traffic. If a new field is optional it's ignored by older consumers; if a field changes type we surface regression alerts tied to eval prompts.
[12:30] Liam: Can you demo a guardrail failing and how the system responds?
[12:35] Marcus: Sure — I'll force a malformed response.
[12:40] [runs malformed sample]
[12:46] Marcus: The system rejected the response, logged the error, and returned a structured error to the caller. I can toggle repair mode — when enabled it sends a repair prompt to the model to reformat. See the latency increase in Console for that request.
[13:00] Priya: Understood. We prefer reject + alert rather than silent repair for critical writes.
[13:06] Marcus: That's a common preference for finance/analytics workloads.
[13:10] Sofia: Quick show of SDK — one line to enable JSON mode and attach schema, another to declare function handler endpoints.
[13:20] Marcus: Example pseudo call: Redwood.generate({mode: 'json', schema: 'v2-order-schema', functions: [...]}) — you can also stream and still validate per-chunk if you want partial outputs.
[13:36] Jorge: Streaming + validation — what's the guarantee? If a stream starts valid but ends malformed?
[13:42] Marcus: We validate final payload at end of stream; you can also configure incremental validation and fail fast. Streaming is more complex, we show tradeoffs in Console's docs.
[13:55] Nia: Are there client libraries for our stack? We use Python/Node and a Go internal toolchain.
[14:01] Sofia: Yes: official SDKs for Python, Node, and Go; plus examples for serverless webhooks. Marcus will share code snippets.
[14:10] [20 min mark — Console tour continues]
[20:05] Marcus: Console shows per-route token cost, 95th percentile latency, and a heatmap for schema errors. You can set alerts on thresholds and wire them to Slack or PagerDuty.
[20:22] Ava: We also have rollout controls: canary percentage, automatic fallback to a known-good model variant if error rate crosses threshold, and auto-scaling policies for Dedicated capacity.
[20:36] Priya: For our compliance team we need SSO with SAML + RBAC.
[20:40] Marcus: Supported — SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC for Console. We'll include sample SAML metadata in the security pack.
[20:52] Liam: Cool. Also interested in per-token billing granularity and how caching impacts cost allocation across teams.
[21:00] Sofia: Console breaks cost by token, route, and model; Optimize suggests cache policy changes and batching to reduce unit cost.
[21:08] Jorge: Can Optimize generate batching configs automatically for us?
[21:13] Ava: It will recommend batching windows and target sizes based on observed QPS and latency SLOs. You can accept suggestions or tweak them per-route.
[21:25] Priya: Security question: what's your SOC2 coverage and do you share audit logs?
[21:30] Marcus: We are SOC2 Type II certified; we provide audit logs and can map events to our control framework. For Private deployments we can integrate with your SIEM. We'll attach SOC2 report in the security pack.
[21:45] Liam: For pilot sizing — what do you need from us?
[21:49] Sofia: Sample prompts, expected QPS, target latency SLOs, and a small set of golden responses for evals. We'll run a 2-week pilot with benchmarks.
[21:59] Liam: Ok we'll send that.
[22:02] [mid-call — more Q&A and small off-topic chatter]
[30:00] Marcus: Running a scenario: intent classification -> function call -> enrichment -> DB upsert. I'll show the full trace and the JSON payload going to your enrichment webhook.
[30:20] [model run shows confidence threshold routing to manual review]
[30:34] Marcus: In this case confidence was 0.58, so policy routed to manual review. Console surfaced it in the queue and notified the review team.
[30:50] Nia: Nice. How fast is manual review throughput? We have a team of 3 with SLA to clear 500/day.
[30:58] Marcus: You can tune review batch sizes and assign reviewers. For high throughput we suggest a hybrid auto-approve for high-confidence plus a smaller human review sample.
[31:10] Priya: What about data residency — we have EU customers and need certain data to stay in eu-west-1.
[31:16] Marcus: You can pin routes to regional hosts and use private deployment in an EU region. We'll show deployment region controls in Console.
[31:30] Sofia: Quick note on cost modeling — we'll provide an expected TCO for hosted vs dedicated for your projected traffic.
[31:38] Liam: Great.
[31:40] [40 min mark — demo wrap-up]
[40:05] Marcus: Final notes: we log request and response metadata, but you can opt to redact or not store the content. Private deploy gives you full control.
[40:16] Sofia: Do you have any remaining blockers to proceed to pilot?
[40:20] Priya: Security review timeline — we need SOC2 docs and KMS details. Also we need a statement about data deletion/retention for PII.
[40:30] Marcus: We'll include a data retention section in the security pack and a deletion playbook for the pilot.
[40:38] Liam: Also want to validate that the SDKs support our auth flow (OIDC + mTLS).
[40:45] Marcus: SDKs support OIDC; mTLS is supported for Private endpoints. We'll add example configs.
[40:52] Nia: On success criteria for pilot: 1) Schema pass rate > 99% on golden prompts, 2) P95 latency under 150ms for enrichment route, 3) No PII written to logs.
[41:05] Sofia: Perfect — we'll use those as pilot success metrics in the SOW.
[41:12] Priya: Anything else about rollback or incident response?
[41:16] Marcus: Console has per-route automatic fallback and built-in tracing to troubleshoot. We'll include our incident runbook for Dedicated/Private customers.
[41:27] [closing minutes — recap and next steps]
[41:30] Sofia: Recap: We'll send pilot SOW and pricing (Sofia), security pack and SOC2 (Marcus), example schema (Ava). Customer to send sample prompts and traffic estimates (Liam). Aim to kick off week of 2027-08-16.
[41:49] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks for the demo.
[41:53] Sofia: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and attachments.
[42:00] [call ends]

Notes on transcript quality: automated captions had a few misattributions and small transcription errors around product names like "KV cache" appearing as "K V cache" and "quantization" split into two words; we've preserved spoken hesitations and interruptions.
